newsitem.title: USA: Witnesses in funds scandal to be offered immunity.
newsitem.headline: Witnesses in funds scandal to be offered immunity.

text.p: The Senate committee investigating campaign fund-raising scandals will vote Thursday on a Republican proposal to offer a dozen witnesses immunity from prosecution in exchange for their testimony.

Sources close to the Senate governmental affairs committee said the witnesses were "lower level players who said they would not testify unless they received immunity and who could supply valuable information to the investigation."

The sources said committee chairman, Sen. Fred Thompson of Tennessee, would supply the names of those to be offered immunity to Democrats on the committee by Wednesday. The sources declined to name the individuals involved.

The committee was investigating whether China and other foreign interests sought to influence U.S. foreign policy by helping President Bill Clinton and the Democratic Party with illegal political contributions in the 1996 election.
The Democratic Party has promised to return some $3 million which were apparently illegally raised from foreign interests, mainly Asian corporations and businessmen.

Some Republicans believe that Democratic Party fund-raiser John Huang, a former Commerce Department official, may have passed classified trade information to the Indonesian-based Lippo Group, identified as the source of some of the illegal funds which he raised.

The vote Thursday will be a test of relations between the majority Republicans and the minority Democrats on the committee, which have sharply deteriorated in recent weeks. A total of 11 votes would be needed to grant immunity to witnesses. Republicans only have nine votes and would therefore need at least two of the seven Democrats to join them.

Democrats would like to probe Republican financial links to foreign business interests. The Republicans have returned some $122,000 raised for a party think tank from a Hong Kong company and Democrats believe they have much more to hide.
In an angry letter to Thompson Monday, ranking Democratic Sen. John Glenn of Ohio said the investigation had turned into a witch hunt of Democrats while Republicans were being shielded from scrutiny.

Many key players in the scandal have either gone to Asia or, like Huang, have indicated their intention of taking the Fifth Amendment, which gives them the right to remain silent to avoid self-incrimination.

The granting of immunity in exchange for congressional testimony is a delicate matter. In the 1980s, some key players in the Iran-Contra scandal eventually escaped punishment because they were given immunity by Congress.
